title: Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide
summary: On 9 December 1948, the United Nations General Assembly unanimously adopted the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide at the Palais de Chaillot in Paris. Prompted by Raphael Lemkin's tireless advocacy following the Holocaust, the convention became the first United Nations human rights treaty, codifying genocide as an independent crime under international law and obligating signatory states to prevent and punish acts committed to destroy national, ethnical, racial, or religious groups.

where.historical_name: Palais de Chaillot, Paris, French Fourth Republic (Third Session of the United Nations General Assembly)

importance.justification: The Genocide Convention was the inaugural human rights treaty adopted by the United Nations, establishing the foundational global legal framework defining and prohibiting genocide.

audience_note: Discusses the international legal definition of genocide, involving mass atrocities, extermination, and physical or cultural destruction targeting national, ethnic, racial, or religious groups.
